title: Infertility and Childlessness: The Ache of Empty Arms
subtitle: The grief that arrives monthly and announces nothing, the friends whose pregnancies become small funerals, the church that does not know what to say. A Christian reckoning with the longing for a child that goes unanswered, the women of Scripture who waited, and the hope and identity that must be found when children do not come.

connections.label: This is grief, even when there is no body to bury. The loss that has no funeral has its own page.
When children do not come, the question of who you are without them grows loud. Identity has its own page.
The monthly ache feeds an anxiety that hope deferred makes worse. The anxious mind has its own page.
Infertility strains a marriage in ways nothing else does. The long covenant has its own page.
A full life without biological children is not a lesser life. Singleness and fruitfulness without children share a page.

parts.title: The Grief That Comes Every Month
parts.body:
You know the calendar in your body before you know it in your head. There is a date you do not write down and cannot forget, and as it approaches a hope you swore you would not feel begins to rise anyway, quietly, against your will. And then it comes, the sign you dreaded, and the hope dies again, and no one in the world knows that a small grief just happened in your bathroom. You wash your face. You go to work. You smile at the person in the next office who is asking when you two are going to start a family, and you say something light, and you carry the funeral inside you all day long.

This is the loneliest grief I know, because it has no body and no date and no one to receive the condolences. When someone dies, the world stops for a moment. Casseroles arrive. People say they are sorry. There is a service, a marker, a permission to weep. Infertility has none of that. It is a death that happens over and over, monthly, privately, with no funeral and no flowers, and the world does not even know to be sorry, because the thing you lost was never a person anyone but you could see. You grieve a face you have only imagined, a name you have only whispered, a child who exists nowhere but in the ache.

And the ache is everywhere, because the world is full of babies. The pregnancy announcement at the dinner table that you have to be happy about while something inside you folds in half. The baby shower invitation that arrives like a summons. The friend who complains about her morning sickness while you would trade every comfortable year of your life for one morning of it. The church nursery you cannot walk past. The Mother's Day service that becomes, for you, the hardest hour of the year, when you sit in the pew while mothers stand to be honored and you stay seated, invisible, holding a grief the whole congregation is celebrating its way right past.

Let me say the thing the well-meaning people get wrong, because their clumsiness has wounded more aching couples than their silence ever could. This is not a problem to be solved with their advice. Just relax and it will happen. Have you tried. My cousin adopted and then got pregnant right away. You can always adopt. Maybe it is not God's timing. Every one of those sentences, offered to fix the unfixable, lands as a small cruelty, because it treats a deep grief as a glitch and turns the sufferer into a project. You do not want their solutions. You want someone to sit in the ache without trying to make it go away.

We have a church that knows how to celebrate the family and does not know how to grieve with those for whom the family will not come. It has a Mother's Day and no day for the empty arms. It has a fertility it preaches as a blessing and a barrenness it does not know how to name. And so the infertile sit in the middle of the very community that should hold them, more alone there than anywhere, smiling through the announcements, grieving a child no one will ever meet, carrying a loss the church does not know how to mourn.

parts.title: Why This Grief Deserves to Be Named
parts.body:
It matters because the longing for a child is not a trivial want, and treating it as one is a wound. This is not someone failing to get a thing they merely prefer. The desire to bear and raise a child is woven into the body and the soul at a depth few other desires reach, a longing as old as Eve, who named her firstborn with a cry of having gotten a child from the Lord. To want a child and be unable is to feel a part of yourself that was made for something it cannot do, and the grief of that is proportionate to the depth of the design. It deserves to be named as the real and heavy loss it is.

It matters because of what unnamed grief does when it has nowhere to go. The couple who cannot speak their loss, who have no language for it in their church and no permission to weep, do not stop grieving. They grieve underground, alone, often separately, and the grief that cannot be shared turns into isolation inside the very marriage that should be its shelter. Infertility breaks couples, not because the diagnosis is too heavy but because the silence is, because two people can be lying in the same bed grieving the same child and never reach each other across the dark. A grief named together can be borne. A grief hidden corrodes.

It matters because of the lie that grows in the silence, and it is a spiritual lie. In the quiet, the aching heart begins to whisper that this is a verdict. That God is withholding. That a barren womb means a deficient faith, a hidden sin, a soul somehow less favored than the friend whose house is full of children. The prosperity-shaped corners of the church feed this lie directly, suggesting that enough faith would open the womb, which is a cruelty dressed as encouragement and a heresy that turns a medical condition into a moral failure. The infertile heart, left alone with that whisper, can come to believe that God himself has rendered a verdict on its worth, and that lie has to be killed before it kills hope.

And it matters because the watching world is paying close attention to exactly this. The skeptic does not doubt that Christians can be happy when life is going their way, when the prayers are answered and the houses fill with children. He doubts that the faith holds when the prayer is not answered, when the deepest, most natural, most God-honoring desire of a heart goes unmet year after year. A couple who walks through infertility and does not lose their faith, who grieves honestly and worships anyway, who finds their identity and their hope intact even with empty arms, testifies to something the world cannot explain, that the love of God is not a transaction that pays out in babies but a presence that holds you when the thing you longed for never comes.

parts.title: What Scripture Says to the Barren and Waiting
parts.body:
Begin where so many aching couples are afraid to look, with the fact that Scripture is full of women who could not conceive, and that God did not look away from a single one of them. Sarah waited until laughter seemed the only honest response. Rebekah was barren until Isaac pleaded for her. Rachel cried out give me children or I shall die, naming a desperation the polite church no longer permits. Hannah wept until the priest thought she was drunk, praying with a bitterness of soul she did not hide from God. Elizabeth bore the reproach of childlessness into old age. The mother of Samson, the Shunammite woman, the women whose names we know and the ones we do not. The Bible does not treat barrenness as a rare misfortune to be glossed over. It puts it at the very center of its story, again and again, as if God meant for the childless to know they were seen.

And look closely at Hannah, because she is the patron saint of every couple grieving in a pew. She did not pretend. She did not say the right pious thing. She went to the house of God in anguish and wept and prayed out of great anxiety and vexation, and she poured out her soul before the Lord. When the priest accused her of drunkenness, she answered that she was a woman troubled in spirit, pouring out her soul. Scripture honors her honesty. It does not rebuke her grief or tell her to relax or count her blessings. It records her raw lament as faith, not the absence of faith, because the deepest faith is not the kind that feels nothing. It is the kind that brings the whole unedited ache to God and refuses to take it anywhere else.

Scripture is also dangerously honest about what infertility does between people, and it does not flinch from the failures. Sarah, in her grief, drove Hagar into Abraham's bed and then drove her into the wilderness, and a household tore apart over a barrenness no one knew how to bear. Rachel turned her envy on her sister and her bitterness on her husband. The Bible shows us that the longing for a child, when it is not surrendered to God, can curdle into envy, manipulation, and cruelty, and it shows us this not to condemn the childless but to warn them, gently, that the unsurrendered ache is dangerous, that the desire for a good thing can become an idol that demands a sacrifice, and that the only safe place for a longing this deep is the open hand before God.

Then Scripture does something the fertility-obsessed reader almost always misses. It severs the link between barrenness and worth, decisively, and it does so at the cross. The most fruitful human being who ever lived left no biological children. Jesus of Nazareth, in whom all the families of the earth are blessed, had no son to carry his name, and his name fills the earth. Paul, who fathered churches across the empire, fathered no children of his own flesh. And the prophet Isaiah, speaking to the barren woman, says something that should be read at every infertile bedside. Sing, O barren one, who did not bear, for the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married. The God of Scripture refuses to measure a life by the wombs it filled. He measures it by the love it bore and the lives it touched, and by that measure the childless can be more fruitful than the fertile, and often are.

And Scripture offers, in the end, an identity and a hope that no biological loss can reach. To the eunuch, the man who could never father a child, who might have thought himself a dry tree cut off from God's people, Isaiah gives the most tender promise in the Bible. To them I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off. God offers the childless not a consolation prize but a deeper belonging, a name in his house that outlasts any family line, a place in a family that is not built on blood at all. The Christian hope was never finally that you would extend yourself through your children. It was that you would be a child, adopted, named, and kept, in a Father's house where no one is barren and no arms stay empty forever, where the One who left no children of his own has prepared a place for all of his, including you.

parts.title: How the Church Has Held the Childless
parts.body:
The ancient world treated childlessness as a catastrophe and often a disgrace, and it usually blamed the woman. In a society without pensions or insurance, children were survival, the only security for old age and the only way a name survived death. A barren woman was not merely sad. She was, in the eyes of her culture, a failure and a liability, and she often bore the shame alone while her husband took a second wife or a concubine. This is the brutal world into which Scripture spoke its tenderness toward the barren, and the gentleness of the biblical witness stands out sharply against the cruelty of the surrounding cultures, a deliberate mercy aimed at the most despised.

The early church carried something genuinely new into that world, a community where worth was not measured by fertility. The first Christians honored virgins and widows, people who bore no children, as full and valued members of the family of God, sometimes as its most honored. The church taught that the deepest kind of fruitfulness was spiritual, that a person who never bore a child could be a mother or father to many in the faith. The desert mothers and fathers, the unmarried teachers and saints, became spiritual parents to generations, and the tradition named them so. To be called father or mother in the early church was often to be called it by people one had never physically borne, and the title was not a metaphor but a recognition of real and costly fruitfulness.

The monastic movement made this visible on a vast scale. For most of Christian history, some of the most influential lives were lived by people who chose or accepted childlessness for the sake of the kingdom. The monk and the nun bore no children and yet shaped civilizations, copied the Scriptures, fed the poor, healed the sick, and discipled the young. The tradition never treated their childlessness as a lack to be pitied. It treated it as a different and equally real form of generativity, a life poured out and multiplied in ways that biology cannot. This is a witness the modern church, drunk on the imagery of the nuclear family, has badly forgotten, and the infertile couple is the first to suffer from the forgetting.

The medieval church surrounded its childless with a communion of saints who understood. It gave Hannah and Elizabeth and the mother of Samuel a place in the imagination of the faithful, and it taught that the prayers of the barren were not lesser prayers. Anne, traditionally remembered as the mother of Mary and herself believed to have waited long for a child, became a figure to whom the childless prayed, a sign that the church wanted the aching to know they had company among the holy. Whatever one makes of the particular devotions, the impulse was right, the refusal to let the childless grieve as those without a witness.

And the church must reckon honestly with its modern failures, because they are real and they wound. The prosperity gospel of the last century turned barrenness into a faith deficiency, telling desperate couples that enough belief, enough seed-money sown, enough positive confession would open the womb, and when the womb stayed closed it left them doubly crushed, grieving the child and now also their own supposed lack of faith. This is a false gospel and a cruelty, and it must be named as such. The wiser tradition has always known better, that the God who closed and opened wombs in Scripture did so according to a purpose no formula can command, that faith is not a lever that pries blessings out of God, and that the childless are not under a verdict but inside a mystery, held by a Father whose love for them was never measured by their fertility and never will be.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Infertility has been studied by medicine and psychology, and grief has been mapped by people who are not believers, and much of what they have learned is true and worth receiving with gratitude. All truth is God's truth, and a couple in this valley should take help from honest sources. But every account of this loss carries a buried picture of what a person is and what a life is for, and that picture has to be tested. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and weighs each against Scripture.

secular.source: Reproductive medicine and the fertility industry
secular.author: The field of assisted reproductive technology
secular.whatItGetsRight: Modern medicine has named infertility as a real, often treatable physical condition rather than a curse or a character flaw, and this is a profound mercy. It has given many couples accurate diagnoses, real options, and, often, the child they longed for. It has lifted the ancient shame off the barren by showing that the cause is biological and not moral, and a Christian should be grateful for the genuine gift that medicine has given to countless aching homes.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Medicine can sometimes open the womb and can never answer the deeper question of a person's worth when it does not. The fertility industry, left unexamined, can also intensify the very idolatry Scripture warns against, framing a child as a product to be obtained by enough money, technology, and determination, until the longing hardens into a grasping that consumes a marriage and a savings account and a soul. Scripture honors the use of means and refuses to let the means become a master. It blesses the couple who seeks help and insists that their identity, their hope, and their peace cannot finally rest on a procedure, because a heart that must have a child to be whole is a heart serving something that cannot save it.

secular.author: Elisabeth Kubler-Ross and grief researchers
secular.whatItGetsRight: The study of grief gave the world permission to mourn losses that have no funeral, and it named the particular pain of disenfranchised grief, the sorrow that society does not recognize and therefore does not comfort. Infertility is a textbook case, a real and recurring bereavement with no body and no ritual, and the research that validates it as genuine grief has helped many couples stop apologizing for their tears and start mourning honestly. This is true and humane and good.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The grief literature legitimizes the mourning and stops at the edge of hope. It can give the couple permission to grieve and cannot give them anything sturdy to grieve toward, no horizon beyond the loss. Scripture commands lament, gives Hannah her unedited anguish, and then does what the research cannot, anchoring the grief in a hope that is not wishful, a God who turns mourning into dancing and who has prepared for the childless a name better than sons and daughters. The believer grieves, but not as those who have no hope. The science honors the tears. Only the gospel tells you they are not the end of the story.

secular.source: The childfree movement and the critique of pronatalism
secular.author: Contemporary writers on chosen childlessness
secular.whatItGetsRight: A body of modern thought has rightly challenged the assumption that a life without children is automatically a diminished life, and it has named the cruelty of a culture that treats parenthood as the only path to a meaningful existence. For the involuntarily childless, this critique can be a real comfort, a reminder that a full, generative, deeply worthwhile life is genuinely possible without biological children, and that the ache they feel is partly the pressure of a pronatalist culture and not only the loss itself.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The critique frees a person from the idol of children and can tip into a different falsehood, that the longing itself was always merely cultural, a piece of conditioning to be discarded rather than a grief to be honored. Scripture will not let either lie stand. It refuses to measure worth by fertility, severing the link decisively at the cross, and it also refuses to call the desire for a child an illusion, treating it instead as a real and good longing planted by God. The believer holds both, that a childless life can be gloriously fruitful and that the unmet desire is a true loss worth grieving. The movement is right to deny the idol. It is wrong when it denies the grief.

secular.source: Marriage and family therapy on the strain of infertility
secular.author: Clinicians studying couples in fertility crisis
secular.whatItGetsRight: Therapists have documented with great care how infertility wounds a marriage, how the relentless cycle of hope and loss, the medical interventions, and the differing ways partners grieve can drive a husband and wife into isolated, separate pain inside the same home. They have taught couples to grieve together, to communicate across the difference, and to protect the marriage from being consumed by the pursuit of a child. This is wise, evidence-based, and genuinely protective of marriages under enormous strain.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The therapy describes the strain accurately and treats the marriage as the highest thing to be protected, with the relationship itself as the final good. Scripture agrees the marriage must be guarded and locates its strength somewhere deeper than the marriage. A husband and wife will not finally find their way back to each other across the dark of infertility by communication techniques alone, but by a shared surrender to a God outside the marriage who holds them both. The covenant is protected best not when the couple makes it the center but when together they make Christ the center, and discover they can grieve in the same direction because they are both looking, through the loss, at the same faithful Father.

secular.source: Positive psychology on meaning and generativity
secular.author: Erik Erikson and researchers on generativity
secular.whatItGetsRight: Erikson named generativity, the deep adult need to care for and invest in the next generation, as a real and central human task, and the research confirms that people who pour themselves into the young flourish and those who turn only inward stagnate. For the childless, this points to a true and hopeful path, that the drive to nurture and shape the next generation can be met richly through teaching, mentoring, aunting and uncling, taking in children who need a home, and spiritual parenthood. The need is real, and it has many doors, not only the biological one.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research recovers an old Christian truth and grounds it in the self's need for fulfillment rather than in love. Scripture knew long before Erikson that the childless can be abundantly fruitful, that Paul fathered churches and Jesus fathered a whole new humanity without biological children, but it sets that fruitfulness on a different foundation. The believer does not mentor the young primarily to satisfy a developmental need but to love them as Christ loved, pouring out without requiring the return that fills a personal lack. The generativity is real, the doors are many, and the deepest of them open not from the self reaching for fulfillment but from the self set free to give, the way the One who had no children of his own gave everything for his.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Believers who share the same Scripture and the same grief still disagree about how a couple should respond to infertility, and the disagreement is serious and pastoral, not careless. It runs to the question of how far to go in the pursuit of a child, of where faithful longing ends and grasping begins. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to honor God in an agonizing place, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Pursue every faithful means available to have a child
views.body: This view holds that the longing for a child is a good gift from God and that pursuing it through medicine, treatment, and every ethically faithful means is itself an act of faith and stewardship. God gave humanity the command to be fruitful and the wisdom to develop medicine, and to use that wisdom in the service of a holy desire is to honor him, not to grasp at his prerogatives. Advocates point to the women of Scripture who did not passively wait but acted, who prayed with desperate persistence like Hannah, whose husbands pleaded with God like Isaac, and they argue that the God who often opened the womb in response to fervent prayer and human effort honors the couple who refuses to give up easily on so good a thing. To surrender prematurely, this view warns, can be a false piety that mistakes resignation for trust, that gives up on a good gift God may yet intend to give and calls the giving up spirituality. The danger they are guarding against is a passivity that hides behind theology, a couple who stops pursuing the child God might have given them and dresses their discouragement in the language of acceptance. Against that, they hold that faith is active, that the use of means honors the Giver, and that a couple may pursue a child with everything ethical at their disposal while still holding the outcome, in the end, in an open hand before the God who alone gives life.

views.view: Hold the longing in an open hand and beware the grasp
views.body: This view agrees the desire for a child is good and warns that a good desire pursued without limit becomes an idol that devours. It points to Sarah and Rachel, whose unsurrendered longing curdled into manipulation and cruelty and tore households apart, and it argues that the deepest spiritual danger of infertility is not giving up too soon but grasping too hard, letting the pursuit of a child consume the marriage, the finances, the peace, and the soul, until the couple has made a child into the thing that must be obtained for life to be worth living. Advocates note that Scripture never makes a child a right to be seized and always treats the womb as God's to open, that the most fruitful saints bore no children, and that the work of faith in infertility is often the costly surrender of the deepest desire into the hands of God. To pursue without limit, this view warns, can become a slow idolatry that wounds the marriage it claims to serve. The danger they are guarding against is the couple consumed, who have made the child an ultimate thing and lost their joy, their rest, and sometimes their faith in the relentless pursuit of it. Against that, they hold that the safest place for a longing this deep is the open hand, that real trust may mean ceasing to grasp, and that a couple can pursue a child faithfully only when they have first surrendered the demand for one, holding the desire without letting it hold them.

parts.title: What the Empty Arms Form in You
parts.body:
Infertility forms a person in ways nothing else can, and the forming is not optional. The long ache, the monthly grief, the hope deferred that the proverb says makes the heart sick, all of it is pressure, and pressure shapes. The question is never whether infertility will form you, but into what, and God, who wastes no sorrow, means to make of this barren ground something that fertile ground could never grow.

He forms an honesty in prayer that comfortable people never reach. Infertility takes you to the edge of Hannah's prayer, the place where you stop saying nice things to God and start pouring out your soul in anguish and vexation, where the polite religious voice falls silent and the real, raw, desperate cry comes out. And there, at the bottom of the ache, you discover that God receives that prayer as faith. You learn that you do not have to protect him from your grief, that the deepest worship is not pretending to feel fine but bringing the unedited wound to the only One who can hold it, and a person who has prayed Hannah's prayer prays differently forever after.

He forms a freedom from the false gods of fertility and family. The childless are forced to confront a question the easily-blessed can avoid for a lifetime, the question of whether their worth, their meaning, and their hope are really resting on God or were secretly resting on the family they assumed would come. When the family does not come, the foundation is tested, and a couple who lets the testing do its work discovers, painfully and then gloriously, that they were never meant to find their identity in being parents at all, that their name was always written in a Father's house and never in a family line, and they are freed from an idol that the fertile often serve their whole lives without noticing.

He forms a tenderness toward all the unseen grief in the world. The person who has carried a sorrow no one acknowledged, who has smiled through baby showers with a funeral inside, who has learned what it is to grieve where no one comforts, becomes a person who can see the hidden griefs of others. They walk into a room and notice the woman not standing on Mother's Day. They learn to sit in someone's ache without rushing to fix it, because they know exactly how the fixing wounds. The empty arms, strangely, make a person more able to hold others, and some of the most comforting people in any church are the ones who were never comforted in the way they needed and learned, in the silence, how it should have been done.

And he forms a hope that has been to the bottom and found a floor. The infertile couple who keeps walking with God through the unanswered prayer arrives, in time, at a hope that is no longer naive, no longer dependent on getting the thing they wanted, a hope that has stared into the worst of it and found that God was still there, still good, still holding them with arms that will not empty. This is the deepest fruit of the barren ground, a hope purified by fire, and it is a fruitfulness the world cannot account for, the strange flourishing of people who did not get what they longed for and did not lose their God. Isaiah told the barren woman to sing, and the song he gave her was not a song of denial but a song from the far side of grief, the song of a soul that has found in the everlasting name a thing better than sons and daughters, and that has stopped having to pretend in order to mean it.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: This grief is not eased by being explained. It is carried, in small faithful acts, over a long time, under grace. None of what follows will fill the empty arms, and that is not what practice is for. It is for keeping the soul and the marriage and the hope alive through a sorrow that does not have a schedule. Begin with one thing, this week, and let the rest come as you are able.

steps: Pray Hannah's prayer once this week, unedited. Go somewhere alone and pour out your soul to God in the actual words of your grief, with no piety added and nothing held back. He received Hannah's anguish as faith. He will receive yours.

Tell your spouse one true thing about your grief that you have been carrying alone. Infertility isolates two people inside the same loss. Break the silence with a single honest sentence, and let the marriage become a place where the grief is shared rather than hidden.

Give yourself permission to skip one thing that wounds, this week, without guilt. The baby shower, the announcement-heavy gathering. You are not required to bleed in public to prove your love for others. Protecting your heart is not bitterness. It is wisdom.

Find one place in Scripture where God meets the barren, Hannah or Elizabeth or the promise to the eunuch in Isaiah, and sit in it. Let it tell you that you are seen, that this grief is in the Bible, and that God has never once looked away from the empty arms.

Decide, with your spouse and before God, how you will pursue or not pursue treatment, and hold that decision in an open hand. Name together where faithful effort ends and grasping begins for you, and agree to guard the marriage from being consumed by the pursuit.

Find one other couple or person who has walked this valley, and let yourself not be alone in it. The infertile rarely speak, so you may have to ask, but they are in your church, carrying the same silent grief, and a shared sorrow is half a sorrow.

Plan ahead for the hard days, Mother's Day, Father's Day, the friend's due date, before they arrive. Decide what you will do, where you will be, who will know. A grief you have prepared for can be borne. A grief that ambushes you flattens you.

Begin to grieve the imagined child honestly, even with no body and no funeral. Name the loss as loss, to God and to each other. You are allowed to mourn a child you never met. The grief is real because the love was real.

Hunt down and kill the lie that this is a verdict on your worth or your faith. Take it to a pastor or a trusted friend and say it out loud so its power breaks. A closed womb is not a closed heaven. The God who left no children of his own does not measure you by yours.

Open one door of generativity this season. The need to pour into the next generation is real and has many doors, not only the biological one. Mentor, teach, open your home to a child in need, aunt or uncle a niece or nephew with intention. Begin to be fruitful in the ways that are open to you.

Examine, together, whether a child has quietly become an idol, the thing that must be had for life to be worth living. If it has, the surrender of that demand into God's hands is the hardest and most freeing work of this season. Do it slowly, with help, and with grace.

Let the church hold you, even though it does not always know how. Tell one trusted leader what you are carrying, and ask for prayer and presence rather than advice. You may have to teach the church how to grieve with you, and teaching it is a gift to the next couple.

Build your identity, over this year, on the everlasting name and not on the family line. Return again and again to the truth that you are a child in a Father's house, named and kept, and let that belonging become the floor you stand on whether or not children ever come.

Discern, in time and without pressure, whether adoption or caring for a child in need is a door God is opening, not as a consolation prize but as a calling in its own right. The God who adopted you may be inviting you to adopt, and that family, built by love rather than blood, is no lesser family.

Become, for someone else, the comfort you needed and did not get. Watch for the woman not standing on Mother's Day, the couple grieving in silence, and go sit with them without fixing. Your unhealed-feeling wound may be exactly what makes you able to hold theirs.

Keep singing the barren woman's song for the rest of your life, the song from the far side of grief. Let your life become a testimony the world cannot explain, a couple who did not get what they longed for and did not lose their God, whose arms stayed emptier than they wished and whose hope grew fuller than they imagined, held to the end by the One in whose house no one is barren and no arms stay empty forever.
